Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Queensland have demonstrated an unusual fresh way to communicate, using gravity to send a message directly through a brick wall.
  • Recent findings suggest that the experiment took place inside UQ's Parnell Building.
  • In a recent development, on the other side of a brick wall, a device called a gravimeter was positioned in a nearby bathroom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Queensland have demonstrated an unusual fresh way to communicate, using gravity to send a message directly through a brick wall. Instead of relying on radio waves or other electromagnetic signals, the team used an old elevator, a massive counterweight, and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in gravitational pull.

Recent findings suggest that the experiment took place inside UQ's Parnell Building. Physicists repeatedly moved an elevator between two floors, shifting its 1.8-metric-ton counterweight between two positions. Each position represented a binary digit, either 0 or 1, allowing the researchers to encode information through the movement of the heavy mass.

In a recent development, on the other side of a brick wall, a device called a gravimeter was positioned in a nearby bathroom. The instrument measured the extremely small changes in gravity produced by the moving counterweight. By decoding those measurements, the team successfully recovered a one-word message: 'Gravity'.

Why Gravity Could Succeed Where Wi-Fi Fails.

It has been revealed that the experiment highlights a potentially key advantage of using gravity for communication. Unlike conventional wireless signals, which can be weakened or blocked by physical obstacles, gravitational fields pass through ordinary materials without being screened out.

Sources indicate that dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ's School of Mathematics and Physics explained why this property makes gravity an intriguing alternative to existing communication technologies.

"Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," Dr. Woffinden said.

"Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

"While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.".

The basic principle is surprisingly simple. Any object with mass produces a gravitational field, and moving that object changes the field around it. Although these changes are generally far too small for people to notice, sufficiently sensitive instruments can detect them. By controlling how a large mass moves, researchers can create a sequence of gravitational changes that represents digital information.

From Weighing Trucks to Sending Messages.

The idea for the experiment emerged from a separate research effort that had little to do with communication.

Dr. Andrew Groszek remarked the team had originally been developing a contactless weighbridge, a system designed to measure the weight of vehicles without requiring them to drive onto a conventional scale.

"We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull," Dr. Groszek remarked.

"Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.".

That realization opened the door to a different application. If a sensitive detector could measure the gravitational influence of a large vehicle, it could also detect deliberately controlled changes in the position of a heavy object. Those changes could then be used to represent the ones and zeros that form the foundation of digital communication.

Despite its success, the demonstration revealed a major obstacle to practical gravity-based communication: transmitting information this way is extraordinarily slow.

Professor Andrew White explained that the elevator's age and limited speed placed a severe restriction on how rapidly the researchers could send their message.

"Our lift was snail-paced - it's from the 1950s - so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," Professor White stated.

For comparison, a bit is the smallest unit of digital information, representing either a 0 or a 1. Modern communication systems transmit enormous numbers of bits every second. The gravity experiment, by contrast, required an entire minute to communicate just one bit.

According to White, improving the system would require finding ways to produce detectable gravitational changes more promptly.

"The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.

"It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.".

Could Quantum Sensors Make Gravity Communication Practical?

Although the experiment relied on a conventional gravity sensor, the researchers believe more advanced technology could eventually make the approach faster and capable of operating over greater distances.

Professor Matthew Davis emphasized that the team's most important achievement was demonstrating that gravity could be used to transmit recoverable information.

"It's not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating," Professor Davis mentioned.

"We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

"Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.".

According to recent reports, quantum sensors exploit properties of quantum physics to make exceptionally precise measurements. In principle, their greater sensitivity could allow researchers to detect much smaller gravitational changes, potentially improving both the range and speed of gravity-based communication.

It has been revealed that however, the team's projections depend on ambitious assumptions, and the suggested performance has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. Even at 15 bits per minute, the system would remain dramatically slower than modern wireless technologies.

Still, the potential applications are intriguing. A sufficiently advanced gravity-based communication system could someday transmit information in environments where radio waves, light, and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

For now, an aging elevator and a gravimeter in a university bathroom have demonstrated something remarkable: information can be carried by changes in gravity and recovered on the other side of a solid wall.

The research was published in Science Advances.

Octopuses Use a Multi-Step Process to Squeeze Into Tiny Spaces

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Squeezing your body into the tiniest possible space is no easy task, but it can be very useful, especially if you’re a soft-bodied creature living in the fiercely competitive ocean.
  • Industry observers note that in a recent study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, researchers uncovered the process octopuses go through to squish themselves into small spaces.
  • The research team set up a tank divided by a transparent acrylic panel with a hole in it, allowing the octopus to move through the hole to the other side.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Squeezing your body into the tiniest possible space is no easy task, but it can be very useful, especially if you’re a soft-bodied creature living in the fiercely competitive ocean. Octopuses are the masters of this kind of contortion, being able to squeeze through just about any opening wider than their beaks. Not only is it an impressive feat, but scientists are interested in this ability because it could aid in the design of biologically inspired robots.

Industry observers note that in a recent study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, researchers uncovered the process octopuses go through to squish themselves into small spaces. Before this, “there [was] no information about how octopuses squeeze through an opening far smaller than the body diameter,” Wen-Tzu Hsing, first author of the study, said in a press release.

The research team set up a tank divided by a transparent acrylic panel with a hole in it, allowing the octopus to move through the hole to the other side. They classified the openings as large or small depending on whether the octopuses would have to squish the stiff cartilage structure that protects their central nervous systems, which the researchers could estimate by measuring the distance between their eyes.

It has been revealed that what surprised the scientists was the slightly different approaches octopuses used when moving through gaps of different sizes. When the gap was on the larger side, the process involved three distinct steps. First, the creatures would explore the hole with their arms. They’d then usually insert two arms through to the other side before threading their other arms and mantle through the hole. Often, this final step involved suckering the arms that led the way to the barrier for increased leverage.

In a recent development, however, when the holes got smaller, the octopuses opted for a four-step process instead. The process was the same up to the second stage—where several arms were threaded through the opening—but the subsequent movements differed slightly. For a smaller opening, the octopus would rotate its body upward and push the bases of the arms that had already passed through deeper into the hole to widen the passage. From that position, it twisted and stretched its arms to feed all of them through. Then, once all appendages were on the other side, the octopus slid its head through, also using its tentacles on the barrier for leverage.

It has been revealed that in the 30 successful attempts to pass through the hole observed in this experiment, the octopuses never used this four-step sequence when presented with the large hole. Additionally, side-view footage confirmed that during the last step of moving through a small opening, the octopus deforms its mantle to reduce its diameter. The octopuses also had a preference for which arms they used for the various steps.

Sources indicate that these experiments were conducted with juveniles from two species, the common octopus and the Maya octopus. The researchers therefore don’t know whether these processes hold true across other octopus species, but beyond the strictly biological world, the researchers suggest that these findings could be useful for the design and control of soft robots.

In environments where the size of passageways cannot be predicted—such as among debris at disaster sites—robots used for search and rescue must be designed to fit through the narrowest passages. Consequently, many existing robots adopt a long, slender, snake-like shape; however, miniaturization inevitably comes at the expense of sensors and operational capabilities. The research team hopes to apply the insights gained from the octopus in this experiment to the control of soft robots designed to search disaster debris or explore difficult terrain.

NASA’s Hubble Views Ocean of Stars in Groundwork for Roman

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that an expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way.
  • According to recent reports, astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail.
  • Hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that an expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way. The images focus on an area of sky toward the galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of a galaxy’s disk. These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

According to recent reports, astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail. Although we can see the glow from these crowded spheres of stars in other galaxies, they are too jam-packed and far away to resolve individual stars. By studying the Milky Way’s galactic bulge, researchers hope to find latest planets and better understand how galaxies form, evolve, and interact over billions of years.

Hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light. Because researchers wish to compare Hubble’s observations to future Roman observations, Hubble looked at the region in wavelengths that overlap with Roman’s areas of sensitivity, the red end of the visible spectrum and near-infrared wavelengths.

Hubble’s high resolution allows its instruments to collect data on the brightness, ages, composition, and motion of stars over time. With this knowledge, astronomers can search for potential exoplanets, determine the location of black holes or dark matter, and better understand our galaxy’s environment and evolution.

A key component of Roman’s future observations is the search for exoplanets by capturing microlensing events, a type of gravitational lensing that occurs when light from a more distant object is magnified and distorted by the mass of a closer object along the line of sight. The way light from the distant star is distorted and magnified can reveal clues to the nature of the foreground star and any planets it may have. Hubble's observations will help characterize stars in the region before they undergo a lensing event. Months or years in the future, when Roman captures a microlensing event, researchers can compare Hubble data to Roman data of the event, making it easer to interpret. These microlensing events are on a much smaller scale, that of stars and planets, than larger gravitational lenses that occur around galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Sources indicate that over Hubble’s lifetime, it has observed our galaxy’s central bulge many times. These legacy surveys include the WFC3 Galactic Bulge Treasury Program that used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 to study the brightness, precise positions, and motions of stars in this congested part of our galaxy. It also includes the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search (SWEEPS) that used Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys to look at 180,000 stars in the bulge of our galaxy. These newly introduced observations come from an observing program (#17776: S. Terry) designed to aid Roman in its search for exoplanets, black holes, neutron stars, and more. The data also adds to Hubble’s continuing legacy of high-precision observations of stars in the galactic bulge.

Claire AndreoliNASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MDclaire.andreoli@nasa.gov.

Since its 1990 launch, the Hubble Space Telescope has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe.

Hubble's most notable scientific discoveries reflect the broad range of research and the breakthroughs it has achieved.

NASA's Hubble and Roman space telescopes will work together to broaden our perspective of the universe.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will settle essential questions in the areas of dark energy, exoplanets, and astrophysics.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German government has presented some grim statistics with regard to misogyny, rape, violence and murder, with reported cases of domestic violence at an all-time high.

At a press conference in Berlin on Tuesday, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig released the latest figures on crimes that specifically target women: whether within families and intimate relationships, in public or online.

In contrast to the statistics pertaining to crime overall, which have remained the same or increased only slightly, reports of crimes against women have increased.

"Behind all these terrible numbers lie individual stories, people and particularly women and girls, whose lives are severely affected by these acts of violence," said Dobrindt.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In 2025, some 280,000 people were victims of physical abuse in their own homes, a 2.8% increase compared to the previous year. Over 70% of the victims were female. Each hour, 16 women are subjected to physical abuse behind closed doors.

The male victims included boys who had been assaulted by their fathers.

The number of misogynistic hate crimes has also risen dramatically, by almost 50%, to 819 cases.

According to recent reports, "The figures show us what it can mean to be a woman in Germany," mentioned Hubig. "It can mean being killed by one's partner or ex-partner. Being a woman can also mean being physically abused by one's partner or ex-partner in one's own home. Being a woman can mean that one's sexual autonomy is brutally disregarded.".

It has been revealed that according to the latest findings, both perpetrators and victims are getting younger. In 2025, nearly half of all female victims of sexual offenses were under the age of 18. And the number of incidents of online violence against women and girls rose by 15.7%. This includes the unauthorized sharing of videos and photos, verbal abuse, manipulation of images, threats and online blackmail, as well as cyberstalking.

Because many perpetrators and victims are still in their teens, Prien, who is also minister for education, said the government wanted to focus primarily on schools, which she explained should become places of prevention.

"Ultimately, we need to bring about a change in people's mindsets, especially those of men. That will be the deciding factor in the end," she mentioned.

In a recent development, over the weekend, Justice Minister Hubig had already announced that in future all femicides, the intentional killing of girls and women because of their gender, would be classified as murders. Presently, such crimes are often classified as manslaughter, for which the penalty is less severe than for murder.

Hubig told German broadcaster ZDF that it was increasingly common that femicides be described as family tragedies or as domestic dramas revolving around jealousy and then classified as manslaughter.

Sources indicate that martina Link, the vice president of the Federal Criminal Police Office, was also at the press conference in Berlin. She called for everybody to pay closer attention to the issue, within their own families, neighborhoods or at work.

Sources indicate that "Violence against women is not a private matter," she stated. "Not in our immediate surroundings nor in the digital world.".

She also pointed out that when it came to sexual offenses and domestic violence, only about 5-10% of cases were reported.

#208015. Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1383 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1383 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again.
  • The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.
  • "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," indicates Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to new research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.

"It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," indicates Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.".

Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History.

In a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago.

In a recent development, at its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains.

Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware.

"People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," states Young.

Scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again.

Answering that question could reveal whether a upcoming cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed.

Sources indicate that (A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.).

Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues.

Sources indicate that piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading.

The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history.

Unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

Since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating.

Industry observers note that this technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice.

These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape.

"If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," claims Young.

Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago.

The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region.

Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change.

Industry observers note that their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.

Young and his colleagues argue that this renewed growth should be recognized as the start of Earth's next glacial period.

That interpretation differs from previous research based on climate models, which has generally suggested that the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

The disagreement partly comes down to how scientists define the beginning of a glacial period. Rather than waiting until enormous ice sheets have spread across continents, Young's team proposes that the first sustained expansion of an existing ice sheet should mark the starting point.

Under that definition, the next glaciation had already begun long before modern scientists recognized it.

The discovery also casts newly introduced light on a controversial scientific debate from the 1970s, when some climate researchers suggested that another ice age might be approaching.

Recent findings suggest that "It actually was happening," Young says. "They couldn't quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence.".

However, this early expansion would not have produced an immediate or dramatic transformation of the planet. According to Young, it would have taken thousands of years for the cooling to become noticeable and roughly 30,000 years for the Laurentide Ice Sheet to regain its enormous continental dimensions.

The process was only in its earliest stages when the warming climate brought it to a halt.

Global Warming Reversed the Growth of the Ice Sheet.

By the 1960s, conditions had changed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during the summer than it could replace through winter snowfall.

Instead of continuing to expand, the ancient ice began shrinking.

According to the researchers' interpretation, this reversal effectively ended the developing glacial period before it could progress into a full-scale ice age.

The consequences may extend far beyond the present day. Models projecting the future of the Barnes Ice Cap indicate that it could disappear entirely within the next few centuries.

"That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young says.

The Loss of an Ancient Ice Cap Could Change Future Ice Ages.

The disappearance of the Barnes Ice Cap could also have implications for how future glacial periods develop.

In the past, the Laurentide Ice Sheet provided a starting point for renewed glaciation whenever Earth's climate cooled sufficiently. Because a large existing mass of ice helps create conditions favorable for further ice accumulation, it can trigger reinforcing processes that allow glaciers to expand.

Scientists describe this kind of process as a positive feedback. In this case, existing ice helps promote the growth of additional ice, allowing an ice sheet to become increasingly extensive as temperatures remain cold.

Without the Laurentide's last surviving remnant, a future glacial period might unfold differently.

Researchers cannot yet determine when another glaciation could begin under atmospheric conditions influenced by elevated greenhouse gas concentrations. If enormous continental ice sheets eventually start forming again, they may have to develop without the ancient ice that previously helped initiate their growth.

The findings suggest that global warming has done more than melt glaciers and shrink existing ice sheets. It may have interrupted a glacial cycle that was already beginning, while also removing a feature that helped sustain ice age cycles across North America for millions of years.

"What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone," claims Young.

'Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home' at 40: 'Trek' has never been as joyous or fun as in 'the one with the whales'

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales".
  • After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief.
  • Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales".

After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp?

Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters.

They gave him freedom to tell the story he wanted to tell, and he landed on a not obviously box-office-friendly formula of "No dying, no fighting, no shooting, no photon torpedoes, no phaser blasts, no stereotypical bad guy". It was a massive shift away from Khan and Kruge, the grandstanding villains in movies II and III.

It has been revealed that nimoy also wanted the film to have an environmental message and appeal beyond the franchise's traditional fanbase. The film would actually be promoted with minimal "Trek" branding in some territories.

Recent findings suggest that "I wanted to make it accessible to people who don't go to 'Star Trek' movies," Nimoy said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman. "I wanted to make it a movie-movie. It starts out like a 'Star Trek' movie and then makes a left turn. It is intentionally very different.".

Recent findings suggest that "The Voyage Home" effectively closes the trilogy that began four years earlier with "The Wrath of Khan". The story picks up three months after Spock's regenerated body is reunited with his katra (spirit), though nobody ever explains why Kirk and the rest of the crew are all still wearing exactly the same clothes. Following the self-destruction of Enterprise over the Genesis Planet, the gang are heading back to Earth to face the music for a lengthy rap sheet that includes grand theft starship and insubordination on an epic scale.

But as they voyage home (geddit?) in a reconditioned Klingon Bird-of-Prey nicknamed the Bounty — complete with a cloaking device that will come in very handy when hiding in Golden Gate Park — they learn that an alien probe of unknown origin (one of the coolest "Star Trek" spaceships) is tearing Earth apart looking for humpback whales. With the species extinct since the 21st century, the crew travel back in time via one of the most surreal sequences in "Star Trek" history — Morphing CG heads? What the hell was Nimoy thinking? — in the hope of finding the whales that might just be able to ask politely if the probe might leave us alone.

Screenwriters Steve Meerson and Peter Krikes were assigned to the project early on (working with Nimoy and producer Harve Bennett on the story), and their treatments included a future Earth under threat from a plague and a discarded subplot about Lt. Saavik being pregnant with Spock's child as a result of the pon farr mating ritual. There were also discussions about the Bird-of-Prey decloaking above the Super Bowl, and — most bizarrely of all — a guest-starring role for Eddie Murphy as an astrophysicist who wants to believe in aliens.

Murphy was both a Trekkie and one of the biggest stars on the planet at the time but ultimately decided to make notorious stinker "The Golden Child" instead. "In retrospect, I think I might have been better off doing 'Star Trek IV'," he said later. Paramount had also gotten cold feet about putting the star of the highly lucrative "Beverly Hills Cop" in its highest-profile franchise.

"Paramount said, 'We're not going to put out [our] two most valuable assets in one movie – so start over, folks!'" said Nicholas Meyer (h/t The Telegraph), hired to retool the script after Murphy's departure. "That's why I was called at the last minute.".

Industry observers note that meyer was already "Star Trek" royalty, having brought the movie series to life as director and uncredited writer of "The Wrath of Khan". Indeed, he's arguably the reason the "odd numbers bad/even numbers good" theory of "Trek" films persisted for so long, having later gone on to co-write and direct "Star Trek VI: The Undiscovered Country".

He shared scripting duties with Bennett, with the producer writing the 23rd-century-set bookends of the film, and Meyer handling everything in present-day California. Weirdly, Meyer had prior experience bringing a time traveler to contemporary San Francisco in his 1979 HG Wells/Jack the Ripper adventure "Time After Time".

Sources indicate that with the three previous "Star Trek" movies largely studio-based, "The Voyage Home" marked a rare chance for cast and crew to head out on location. The Monterey Bay Aquarium filled in for the Cetacean Institute (slightly implausible home of humpbacks George and Gracie), while the USS Ranger — moored in San Diego and no stranger to Hollywood after "Top Gun" — guest-starred as a nuclear "wessel".

According to recent reports, kirk and co. also headed out onto the streets of San Francisco. Nimoy had toyed with giving them '80s-appropriate disguises, but changed his mind when he realized nobody would bat an eyelid at their 23rd-century civilian attire.

Aside from some second unit work photographing humpbacks off the coast of Hawaii, the whales themselves were mostly animatronics created by Industrial Light & Magic. "One of the reasons we think that ['The Voyage Home'] really didn't win visual-effects awards is people didn't really understand how good [the whales were]," said executive producer Ralph Winter. "ILM did such a good job on those whales that they went on tour for a year or more around the world to museums because the expertise, the art, and science of what they had done was very good.".

Meyer, meanwhile, fully embraced the opportunity to write a fish-out-of-water comedy, with this seasoned crew of Starfleet veterans struggling to get their heads around the eccentricities of late 20th-century America.

In a recent development, kirk and Spock experiment extensively with "colorful metaphors" — "double dumbass on you!" — while Kirk gets out of paying for dinner by using the convenient excuse that money isn't a thing in the future. Scotty (James Doohan) attempts to talk to a mid-'80s Apple Macintosh via a mouse before he risks screwing with the timeline by 'inventing' transparent aluminum decades early.

Recent findings suggest that and in the film's most famous moment, Spock delivers a Vulcan neck pinch to a punk playing his music very loudly on a public bus, winning extensive applause from his fellow passengers in the process. The nuisance rocker was played by Nimoy's assistant, Kirk Thatcher, who co-wrote the "I Hate You" song that plays on that era-authentic ghetto blaster. He later returned to the role in "Star Trek: Picard", though this time he responded more apologetically to Seven of Nine's request to turn it down.

In a recent development, kirk is undoubtedly the center of the movie, pulling the strings and getting his first romantic interest since the Original Series — whale expert Dr Gillian Taylor (Catherine Hicks), who eventually accompanies the Enterprisers back to the future. But "The Voyage Home" also gives the supporting bridge crew — all of whom reveal a talent for comedy — more satisfying character beats than they'd ever had before. Walter Koenig's W-heavy pronunciation of "vessels" would later be adopted by Anton Yelchin when he inherited the role in JJ Abrams' "Star Trek".

The crew eventually makes it out of the 20th century alive, with the whales safely secured in a giant fish tank so they can make contact with the probe. Of course, what George and Gracie actually say when they arrive in the future remains a mystery; despite Bennett's insistence that the whale song conversation should be subtitled, he was wisely overruled by Nimoy.

According to recent reports, with Earth saved from death by giant cigar, the Enterprise crew have all their charges revoked, bar one, as Kirk is 'busted' down to Captain. The crew is then gifted the shiny fresh USS Enterprise-A, freeing them to continue exploring the cosmos on the massive screen.

Which they did, with Shatner taking advantage of a so-called "favored nations" clause in his contract — which meant Paramount had to match anything offered to Nimoy — to direct the rather less positively received "Star Trek V: The Final Frontier", before Meyer returned for "The Undiscovered Country".

Nimoy delivered on his promise to appeal beyond the traditional fanbase, and his reward for earning "Star Trek"'s biggest ever box office haul — a record "The Voyage Home" would hold until Abrams went Trekkin' in 2009 — was directing smash-hit comedy "Three Men and a Baby" the following year. The film also paved the way for "The Next Generation", as Paramount realized the franchise's massive potential, but decided they wanted to cash in without paying mega-bucks for the legacy cast.

Hardcore fans will often claim they prefer the more serious themes of "The Wrath of Khan", "First Contact" or even "The Motion Picture" to "The Voyage Home", but "Star Trek" has rarely been as joyous or fun as on this madcap jaunt to the 20th century. "The One with the Whales" really is one for the ages.

'Star Trek: The Voyage Home' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

According to recent reports, richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

Sources indicate that he's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

Industry observers note that the Richat Structure, also known as the “Eye of the Sahara,” is seen from the International Space Station as it orbited above on Nov. 14, 2026. It is an eroded geological dome about 100 million years old created by igneous activity and uplift in the nation of Mauritania. In this type of geologic structure, rocks exposed in the center of the “bullseye” are older than rocks forming the outer rings. This structure measures 45 kilometers (28 miles) across and is made up of igneous and sedimentary rocks.

Or the slats keep falling down, so you have to do that thing where you pull the mattress over your head as you try to shove them back in place (just me?). The Thuma doesn't creak and never slides around. The foam Pillowboard is an additional expense, but it's comfy. Thuma has since added a wood headboard, which is pricier, but that's what I'll probably upgrade to next, since it completes the look. The only downside is how expensive this whole bed frame is (the price has jumped since I first purchased it), but if it helps, the Thuma is made from repurposed wood, and it's UL GreenGuard Gold Certified, meaning low chemical emissions. —Julian Chokkattu.

It has been revealed that thuma made its name with a minimalist wooden bed (our top pick, above) with clean lines and a tool-free assembly process that's no more complex than snapping together Lego bricks. The Signature was introduced in February 2025 as the brand's first fully upholstered bed. The Thuma Signature has the same Japanese wood joinery at its heart for easy assembly, but covers the frame in soft Italian felted wool or performance linen for a decidedly more posh experience. I've been testing the wool version for a few months. It took less than five minutes for me to assemble, and it's very solid and dead silent, with no squeaking whatsoever. The plush headboard upholstery is pillow-soft, and my only problem with it is remembering not to just lay my head directly on it. Best of all, when it's time to move, this bed pops apart in just a few minutes without any bolts or screws. —Martin Cizmar.

DreamCloud (queen, with bamboo headboard).

I really admire Japanese joinery bed frames, not just because of their minimalistic beauty but also their easy, tool-free setup. Trust me, we don’t want my clumsiness around sharp objects. Not all bed frames that follow this blueprint are of the same caliber, with some being far more stable than others, and the price point usually reflects that. DreamCloud's bamboo Japanese joinery bed frame wasn’t just gorgeous, but outfitted with small details that make a big impact. These include tiny additional rods on each of the boards, located where they are stacked atop each other at the ends. The idea is to keep each of the rails that make up the frame even more secure than just the tension of the overall design. There are included foam blocks if you decide to throw in a headboard, so there's no banging against the wall, either. Plus, I’ll never argue with the price tag, which is very within my budget. —Julia Forbes.

Recent findings suggest that I was broker than broke when I got my first apartment more than a decade ago, and this cheap bed frame I bought from Amazon is still being circulated among my younger family members. It's as simple as simple gets, but the steel construction means the frame is durable, and you don't need to add a box spring. The 18-inch model leaves a cavernous space beneath the bed that can accommodate several tote-style storage containers—which could be a blessing or a curse depending on the usual state of your bedroom floor. Just keep in mind that there is no edge whatsoever. This thing is basically a table for your mattress, but it'll get the job done.

Sources indicate that I've tested nearly a dozen different bed frames during my time leading this coverage area for the WIRED Reviews team, and the Saatva Siena is probably the prettiest and most elegant I've ever tried. The leather upholstery just makes it feel so grown-up. It's sexy but not straight out of a dark romance dungeon. It's a statement piece that blends in with my decor. I like the free in-room delivery and the rich smell of leather. However, while the frame itself is exceedingly stable, it does slide around on my hardwood floors (I'm planning on attaching some rubbery grips to the feet to remedy this). My main complaint is that you can see the slats of the frame when you're close to the mattress. From a distance, it looks OK, but the white slats are so obvious up close, if you're looking, that it takes away from the whole put-together effect for me. It's also the perfect awkward height to attract dust bunnies that can be difficult to clean unless you move the bed to sweep or vacuum. Overall, these drawbacks are minor, and I still think this frame is worth your consideration. I'll just cross my fingers that none of my Hinge dates look too closely.

According to recent reports, when the crib phase ends, this is the bed to get. I upgraded my son from a crib that converted into a toddler bed into this actual kids’ bed, and everyone is sleeping better for it. Nestig originally caught my eye for its adjustable crib, and the Nestig Wave Kids Bed shares similar design elements, with its wooden headboard and side panels. This bed frame can be used as either a Montessori-style floor bed or a standard twin, depending on whether you add the legs. It can accommodate a variety of twin-sized mattresses, and my son loves climbing into his bed each night and demanding I lie down with him while we read. The floor bed aspect is handy since I quietly roll out of the bed and onto the floor to escape his grip, and I like knowing that if my son rolled out of bed, he doesn’t have far to go. When it's time to add the legs, I'll have to take the frame apart partially, which is a small con but not a deal-breaker. —Nena Farrell.

Recent findings suggest that small bedroom? Mobility issues? Don’t want to block a window? You might want to consider a low-profile frame. They’re typically under 11 inches high as opposed to around 20 inches for a traditional frame, which means you may not get as much under-bed storage, but for many, the benefits outweigh this drawback. (The Cooper has about 7 inches of clearance off the floor.) I personally have been grappling with not wanting to block a large window with a headboard, and I was curious if a low-profile frame might be the answer. Sure enough, it was—this 38-inch-tall frame hits just 2 inches below the windowsill and looks fantastic. In fact, the minimalist, mid-century-inspired Cooper is practically indistinguishable from similar frames being sold by Pottery Barn and Crate and Barrel, but runs around $500 less.

With its angled legs and rounded corners, the Cooper definitely has Thuma vibes, but does not feature Japanese joinery construction. It requires some assembly; namely, joining the rails together and screwing down the slats. If you’d rather not deal with this, white-glove delivery is available for $199. For my test unit, it took the delivery driver about 20 minutes to assemble, and in the few months I’ve had it, there haven’t been any squeaks, creaks, or loosening hardware. Note that an 8- to 12-inch mattress is recommended. —Kat Merck.

Industry observers note that if you prefer the look of fabric covers, the Awara Platform frame will be a good fit. It's simple to assemble, and the pieces are easy to move. The spruce wooden slats are all attached together, so once you have the four frame pieces assembled, simply roll the slats out and they'll attach via hook-and-loop closures to the frame itself. The frame's height is nice, too. It's elevated just enough to make your bed look refined, but not so much that you'll end up losing things underneath your mattress. Though be aware, I did seem to stub my toes on this bed frame more than others I've tested.

Recent findings suggest that this adjustable base is from the makers of one of our favorite mattresses overall and one of our favorite mattresses for side sleepers. It runs on electricity to move the hydraulic-like motors below, which raise both the head and foot area of the bed. It comes with a wireless Bluetooth-enabled remote with buttons to adjust the head and foot portion of the bed up and down, a built-in flashlight, and a button to bring the frame down to a flat level.

The Legget & Platt app can act as a remote as well—a huge sigh of relief for a generally scatterbrained person like myself who's prone to losing things. In the app, you name your bed, make the adjustments, and save your favorite positions so you can easily go back to them. The bed frame is sleek—not bulky at all—and is around 13 inches off the ground, making extra storage space underneath that I didn’t have before. The legs are virtually invisible, although the zero-clearance design allows the base to be used without the legs if using platform bases.

The adjustable frame rises in half-inch increments from 13 to 18 inches from the original base, and the motor is fairly quiet. The base works with mattresses designed to flex, without shifting inside materials or weakening the structure, and is compatible with nearly all Saatva mattresses. For non-Saatva mattresses, check with the manufacturer to ensure it's compatible with an adjustable base.

Recent findings suggest that saatva provides a 10-year warranty as well as free in-room delivery and setup, and the deliverymen were done in less than 15 minutes, even putting my old mattress back on for me. I often work in my bed and use pillows to prop me up, and this took away the need to be surrounded by a dozen or so of my favorite body pillows. This customizable frame would work great for those with mobility concerns or health issues like acid reflux, restless leg syndrome, sleep apnea, or sciatica (among other things). This bougie bed base isn’t completely necessary for me, but it’s a fun luxury to have. —Molly Higgins.

In a recent development, this bed frame took me an entire day to build, but it was worth it. It has versions with and without storage, and I chose a storage version to fill the drawers with my various bedding. Adding the storage does nearly double the price and adds to your building time, but the drawers are really useful if it’s something you want. It’s a beautiful bed frame that's felt very stable for the two months I’ve been sleeping on it so far. Even with my questionable building skills, there hasn’t been a squeak when I’m sleeping or getting into bed.

In a recent development, you will want to add on a slatted bed base from Ikea for full support if you don’t have a mattress base already. I really liked pairing this frame with the Lönset slatted bed base for great support on my back. There’s also the cheaper Luröy base if you’re on a budget. —Nena Farrell.

I don't say this lightly or often, but I feel like Silk & Snow could charge much more for this Oeko-Tex-certified bed frame. Assembly was annoying—give me video instructions or give me death!—and slightly fiddly, with many individual pieces that you need to screw in or slot together. But the frame is sturdy, the upholstered fabric is soft and durable, and the slats are nice and supportive. The best feature is the built-in storage drawer, which slides out smoothly and closes tightly with magnets. It strikes the perfect balance of form and function.

It doesn't have as much storage space as the lift-up option we recommend from Castlery, but there's room for spare linens, off-season clothing, or certain unmentionables that you don't want lying around out in the open. Be aware that closing the drawer while your bedmate is sleeping will absolutely jolt them awake. But overall, this affordable bed frame offers a good mix of pleasant aesthetics and practical storage solutions.

According to recent reports, if your bedroom needs decluttering, the Auburn is a worthwhile investment in your mental well-being. Covered in Castlery’s spill-resistant bouclé fabric, the Auburn proved surprisingly durable against my cats, who treat my furniture like their personal playground. Although I was initially worried about the creamy white—a shade most pet owners might avoid—it's still pristine after a month. Aesthetically, I adore the wingback upholstered headboard and low-profile design. The dense-looped Cambria textile is soft without being overly delicate.

My favorite feature, though, is the lift-up storage compartment, ideal for my 700-ish-square-foot apartment. It’s not tall enough for full-size suitcases, but it accommodates all the random items that typically lack a designated spot—duffels, Christmas ornaments, a cat stroller, etc. Castlery offers white-glove delivery, provided the bedroom is ready. Assembly is doable alone, but it’s easier with two people. —Boutayna Chokrane.

Industry observers note that good design is entirely subjective, but I can't get over how pretty this bed frame is. The plush velvet upholstery and padded headboard are stunning and a worthy trade-off if you don't mind the upkeep of cleaning and maintaining upholstered furniture. My tester had to assemble this bed frame herself due to delivery logistics and said it was a massive pain in her nether regions. Typically, this bed comes with white-glove service, where technicians assemble it for you, and she implores you to choose that option if at all possible. The storage is nice and roomy—the bed is being tested by a teenager who likes having extra space to put her ever-growing collections of stuff. The bed is quite sturdy, heavy, and difficult to move, so ensure that any tasks like painting or carpet cleaning are complete, and make sure you know exactly where you want it. For someone looking for an elegant storage bed that will be the centerpiece of their room, this is the perfect option.

It has been revealed that this simple, lightweight bed frame from Quince still has a nice aesthetic touch thanks to the removable linen slipcover. The frame itself is easy enough to move around in case of emergency furniture rearranging, and the removable cover can be spot-cleaned as needed. Just be aware that since it's a platform bed, there's absolutely no storage space to speak of. Our teen tester was bummed they couldn't put their slippers under the bed anymore. Otherwise, though, this frame is nice and effective, with sturdy construction and enough available finishes that it could suit any bedroom.

Sources indicate that silk & Snow Wooden Bed Frame: This stunning frame is easy on the eyes with its rich wood finish, though it was delicate and too easy to scuff for our tastes. The legs didn't wobble, the tool-free assembly was easy, and the frame was solid otherwise, but it's too precious for daily use unless you're really careful (or don't mind the wear and tear).

Nest Bedding Woodland Platform Bed: This no-tools-required frame can be put together and taken apart in minutes. The hook-and-latch design lets you piece the frame into a rectangle quickly. Roll out the slats and you're done. The frame feels sturdy and is available in three different finishes, though there are no returns or trials.

Recent findings suggest that KD Frames Nomad Platform Bed: I've put together two Nomad beds from KD Frames, and I know I've got a few more in me. This simple, sturdy bed frame is made in Athens, Georgia, from tulip poplar. Tulip poplar looks like pine, but it's hardwood, and the twin size of this bed can support 600 pounds. The Nomad has clean lines and comes unfinished, meaning you can easily stain it to fit your other furniture. Best of all, it costs about $300 and can be set up in about 20 minutes. —Martin Cizmar.

Industry observers note that tempur-ActiveBreeze: I’ll go ahead and rip the bandage off—the only way you can get this adjustable frame and enjoy it to its full potential is if you purchase it with its accompanying smart bed, the Tempur-Pedic Tempur-ActiveBreeze. Stick with me, though, as it’s a cooling bed unlike any I’ve seen before. The base contains fans that can blow hot or cold air at three levels within the mattress to disperse along the surface. It’s pricey, but I didn’t wake up sweating once during testing. —Julia Forbes.

Latitude Run Platform Bed Frame: In my quest for finding Thuma dupes, I came across this promising, affordable option on Wayfair. When it first arrived, I wasn’t blown away—the bamboo legs felt too lightweight to adequately hold up heavier mattresses, and tears were shed while assembling the headboard, as it required tools and many, many bolts. The premise of true Japanese joinery frames is that they are tool-free; the headboard didn’t fit the bill here. Once it was up and running, though, it held its own, supporting different mattress types and weights. It didn’t squeak at all, which was shocking. I’m sorry for not having more initial faith in this frame. —Julia Forbes.

How Does WIRED Test Bed Frames?

We used these bed frames exactly like you would. We assembled them ourselves when possible, and we slept on them over the course of weeks, if not months or years. (The minimum time for consideration was one week.) We looked for frames that were durable and worth their cost, taking into account unique features, ease of assembly, and solid construction. Many of these frames are being kept around our homes for long-term durability testing. Frames that aren't kept for long-term testing are donated.

According to recent reports, some brands offer white-glove delivery, where nice folks will come and deliver your bed frame already set up (or, depending on the brand, assemble it in the room of your choice), and then remove the packaging. Sometimes they'll even take your old one (that may come with an upcharge). White-glove delivery is nice, but note that you'll need to make sure the area is completely clear so the delivery people have room to maneuver around.

If you choose to assemble the bed frame yourself, most of the time any tools that are required are included. You might need (or want) to provide your own screwdriver, and you can also expect to use an Allen wrench or a small wrench to tighten down fasteners. Assembly is almost always easier with two people, but it's achievable with one. Be prepared to put out a lot of recycling—there's usually an abundance of cardboard, styrofoam, and other packing material. And if you're pairing your new frame with a new mattress, we have tips on assembly for those, too.

Do You Need a Bed Frame, Headboard, Footboard, or Box Spring?

Technically, you could plop your mattress on the floor and call it a day. But experts recommend using a bed frame for many reasons. Bed frames support your mattress, which in turn helps the mattress last longer by ensuring even weight distribution and preventing challenges like sagging. That added support can help with your sleep quality, too. And they provide circulation under your mattress, which helps eliminate any odors, disperse any heat, and prevent moisture buildup. Finally, bed frames usually provide under-bed storage—and where else are you going to put your seasonal clothes or luggage?

Box springs are hit or miss. Most bed frames nowadays have a solid enough foundation that you don't need to provide a box spring. WIRED's in-house mattress expert, Julia Forbes, has an article where she breaks down exactly when one might be necessary. But if your mattress is made out of certain materials like memory foam with no inner support structure, or your bed frame doesn't have slats to support your mattress, a box spring might be smart. Check with your mattress manufacturer for specific recommendations.

Industry observers note that headboards are purely for aesthetics. You don't need one unless you really want to protect your walls from scuffs, or if you want a place to lean against while you're chilling in bed.

2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1216 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea.
  • It has been revealed that for as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms.
  • According to recent reports, yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

It has been revealed that for as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

According to recent reports, yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a new study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

In a recent development, "In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship.".

Ancient Waterproofing Secrets Revealed.

Industry observers note that since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

"Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions.".

To uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax.

Sources indicate that the team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

One sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

Sources indicate that the addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past.

The sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

Sources indicate that different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

It has been revealed that the pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

The discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean.

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

The stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

Industry observers note that earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an important maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

Sources indicate that the new pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

It has been revealed that the findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

"While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical.".

Childhood, Career Come Full Circle for Budget Analyst at NASA Goddard

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood.
  • Sources indicate that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled.
  • Sources indicate that her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that conversations about NASA were the norm around the dinner table during Ashley Knight’s childhood. Her parents worked at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, and discussions about happenings at the agency continued even when they came home from the office.

Sources indicate that “I remember a poignant dialogue we had after the space shuttle Challenger disaster,” Knight recalled. “However, we talked just as much about the engaging work my parents were doing inside Goddard’s gates.”.

Sources indicate that her father Lyle Knight was a mechanical engineer, while her mother Julia Knight worked the bulk of her career in human resources. They brought their daughter on center for Take Your Child to Work Day and other events, and over time she became hooked.

Recent findings suggest that “I saw the chambers where spacecraft and instruments were being tested, as well as other facilities used to help further space exploration. Above all, I witnessed the passion and collaborative spirit everyone had at Goddard,” Knight said. “As a child, I found it incredibly fascinating.”.

It all came full circle in late August when, after growing up around NASA and later working several contractor roles for the agency, Knight and a number of her colleagues in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer were sworn in as federal employees as part of a workforce directive to strengthen the agency’s technical core competencies by bringing mission-critical positions into the civil service.

Sources indicate that she began her Goddard career more than two decades ago following graduation from the University of Maryland in nearby College Park. As the job search began after commencement, one organization inevitably stood out, along with one particular mission.

When she came across a contractor job opening at Goddard in support of the Hubble Space Telescope team, Knight jumped at the opportunity.

It has been revealed that “Hubble was doing amazing things, and I always admired how they fixed the faulty mirror,” she noted, referring to how astronauts and team members corrected an early spherical aberration during the observatory’s first servicing mission. “It was exciting to become involved with such a flagship mission, especially coming right out of college.”.

As a project support analyst, Knight assisted engineers with test prepares, data gathering, and hardware procurement for Hubble’s fifth and final shuttle servicing mission.

Following the mission’s completion in 2009 and subsequent end of the Hubble shuttle servicing era, she took on a similar role with the Robotic Refueling Mission in what was then the Satellite Servicing Capabilities Office at Goddard – now known as NASA’s In-Space Servicing, Assembly, and Manufacturing Capabilities Office.

According to recent reports, knight left Goddard momentarily afterward to perform contracting work in support of the U.S. Naval Research Laboratory in Washington. After a phone call, she found her way back as a contractor program analyst in the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, helping manage labor budgets within programs by avoiding funding lapses and ensuring employees received their paychecks on time.

Following the August ceremony, Knight now carries the title of budget analyst in the Program Analysis Office within the Goddard Office of the Chief Financial Officer, performing many of the same critical duties as a civil servant.

It has been revealed that “While many functions are similar, transitioning into the civil service makes it easier for my colleagues and I to help keep NASA’s missions going from the financial aspect,” said Knight. “We have more autonomy to perform certain government-related tasks by being on the government side.”.

The civil service also provides additional training and growth opportunities for such positions.

In a recent development, “Ashley is a great team player. This conversion is a fantastic milestone because it unlocks fresh avenues for her learning and development, and allows us to integrate her into new roles,” said Linnette Morales, Knight’s supervisor in the Program Analysis Office. “I am thrilled she can now fully access the opportunities on the civil servant side, immensely benefiting both her continued career growth and our organization.”.

The workforce directive, entitled “Restoring NASA’s Core Competencies” and declared by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in February, is part of a broader effort to expand the agency’s critical institutional knowledge, increase resources essential for mission success, and maintain U.S. leadership in space exploration.

“The directive has given our office an opportunity to rebalance positions across the organization and remove limitations that were applied to those who were previously not government employees,” said Lisa Kelleher, Goddard’s chief financial officer. “We are now better able to insource many of our experienced contractor staff, allowing us to build up our in-house core competencies in areas such as budget analysis and accounting, and in turn increase our support for mission success.”.

For Knight, she sees an increasing importance for her organization and hopes to make impactful contributions, especially as work taking place at Goddard helps NASA return a crewed mission to the lunar surface, build a Moon Base, and eventually send humans to Mars.

Sources indicate that “We’re the go-between between NASA Headquarters and Goddard programs, and it’s our job to make it a seamless transition for projects to use money they’ve been given to help get these projects off the ground,” she stated. “It’s both vital and exciting with the lunar and Mars endeavors, and I’m proud to play whatever role I can.”.

Decades after first following her parents around center, and now following in their footsteps as a NASA civil servant, Knight is as captivated by Goddard and its people as she was during her early visits.

“Through the years, I’ve noticed everyone remains driven by teamwork and achieving the mission,” she said. “Everybody wants to succeed together by working toward the same goal, and I’m grateful I can continue to be part of it all.”.
